name: Magnesium
lead: Magnesium (symbol Mg, atomic number 12) is an alkaline earth metal and an essential mineral that serves as a cofactor for more than 300 enzymes in the human body, including all those that make or use ATP, and it interacts with DNA and RNA [1][2][30]. Roughly half of the body's magnesium is held in bone. It supports nerve and muscle function, energy production, blood pressure and glucose regulation, and is obtained from nuts, seeds, legumes, whole grains, leafy greens and some fruit juices [2][30].

In appearance and physique circles, magnesium is taken as part of a recovery chain: relaxed muscles and better sleep are said to support harder training, which supports muscle gain, while the mineral's role in bone and skin-related physiology is cited as background for general skeletal and tissue health. Magnesium compounds are also used medicinally as laxatives and antacids and, as the sulfate, to treat eclampsia [1]. Epsom salt (magnesium sulfate) baths and topical magnesium oils are a separate, popular way of using the mineral for muscle soreness and skin [31].

As a supplement, magnesium is widely taken for sleep, muscle cramps, relaxation and general bone health. Research describes the strongest role for correcting a deficiency; for other uses, systematic reviews report limited or mixed findings. For sleep, reviews of randomised trials report heterogeneous results, with one meta-analysis in older adults finding shorter sleep-onset latency [3][6][8]. A meta-analysis of 14 trials examined magnesium and muscle fitness [4]. No published study has tested magnesium for altering facial or jaw structure in healthy adults.
Supplements commonly cause loose stools, and people with impaired kidney function can accumulate high levels.

paras: Magnesium salts are used to correct deficiency, as laxatives and antacids (magnesium hydroxide, milk of magnesia), and, as magnesium sulfate, to treat eclampsia and stabilise abnormal nerve excitation [1]. Clinical trials have tested magnesium replacement in critically ill patients, magnesium for post-spinal headache and during scoliosis surgery, and supplementation in chronic kidney disease [23][24][26][11]. A 2021 review covers the biochemistry of magnesium and the social impact of diseases linked to its deficiency [15].

In bone and appearance supplement discussion, magnesium is included as a mineral that influences calcium handling, parathyroid hormone secretion and vitamin D activation, and is incorporated into the surface of bone mineral. This is a skeletal-health rationale; no study has examined magnesium for cosmetic bone change in healthy adults. Magnesium is also taken for sleep and muscle recovery, which people sometimes link to appearance and physique goals.

A 2021 meta-analysis of three randomised trials (151 older adults) found that sleep-onset latency was about 17 minutes shorter after oral magnesium than after placebo, while the authors described the overall evidence as limited [3]. A 2026 systematic review of 12 randomised trials of stand-alone magnesium for sleep described the evidence as mixed, with separate analysis of trials on cramps and restless legs [6]. A 2024 systematic review examined magnesium for self-reported anxiety and sleep quality, noting the supplement's popularity on social media and questioning how far the claims are evidence-based [8]. A trial in adults older than 51 with poor sleep reported improved indicators of magnesium status and inflammatory stress [9]. An open-label crossover trial tested magnesium chloride for depression [10], and a post-hoc analysis examined magnesium with vitamin B6 in stressed adults [12]. A 2024 meta-analysis examined magnesium and cognitive health [7], and a trial of a magnesium L-threonate formula reported improved cognitive function in healthy Chinese adults [14].

A meta-analysis of 14 randomised trials in athletes, untrained adults and older adults or alcoholics assessed magnesium supplementation and muscle fitness outcomes such as strength, power and lean mass [4]. No trial of magnesium for bone outcomes is included in the cited research; its skeletal role is described mainly in physiological terms. A systematic review of supplement bioavailability found that organic magnesium forms appear more bioavailable than inorganic ones and that absorption is dose-dependent, and that all forms can maintain physiological levels in healthy people without a prior deficit [5].

Sleep: meta-analyses and systematic reviews [3][6][8][9] and registered trials of a magnesium supplement for sleep quality and for sleep and cognition in Saudi adults [19][25]. Muscle: a 14-trial meta-analysis [4] and a registered trial of magnesium citrate on hand-grip strength [21]. Mental health and cognition: trials in depression, stress and cognitive function [10][12][14][7]. Cardiovascular and kidney: a randomised trial of magnesium citrate, oxide and sulfate on arterial stiffness [13], the MAGiCAL-CKD trial on vascular calcification in chronic kidney disease [11], and a registered trial on vascular stiffness [22]. Absorption: a registered comparison of oxide and citrate absorption in healthy subjects [20].
No cited clinical trial examines magnesium for jaw, facial bone or other cosmetic outcomes.

Magnesium supplements, particularly oxide and citrate, can cause diarrhoea and abdominal cramping, consistent with the laxative use of magnesium compounds [1]. People with kidney impairment can accumulate magnesium to dangerous levels, and magnesium can interact with certain antibiotics and with bisphosphonates, reducing their absorption. Dietary magnesium from nuts, seeds, legumes and greens is generally considered safe [2]. Diarrhoea is the most common symptom of excess oral magnesium; healthy kidneys excrete the surplus efficiently, so poisoning is rare, and infants should not receive supplements without medical supervision [30].

Good sources include leafy green vegetables, nuts, seeds, dark chocolate, soybeans, bran and whole grains; refining grains removes the magnesium-rich germ and bran, so whole-wheat bread contains about twice the magnesium of white bread [30]. Illustrative figures are about 300 mg in a quarter cup of pumpkin seeds, about 160 mg in chia seeds and about 80 mg in half a cup of boiled spinach [30]. Recommended intakes in the United States are about 400-420 mg per day for adult men and 310-320 mg for adult women, and the tolerable upper intake for supplemental magnesium is set at 350 mg per day in the US and 250 mg in Europe; these limits apply to supplements and drugs, not food [30]. Dietary surveys suggest that roughly 57 percent of US adults fall below the recommended intake [32].

Clinical deficiency is usually driven by medications or illness rather than low intake alone. Loop and thiazide diuretics are the most common drug cause, long-term high-dose proton pump inhibitors and certain antibiotics and chemotherapy drugs can also lower levels, and chronic alcohol use, malabsorption disorders such as Crohn's or coeliac disease, and inherited kidney disorders are recognised causes [32]. Signs include muscle cramps, spasms, tremor, weakness, fatigue, migraines and abnormal heart rhythms, and low magnesium is often accompanied by low potassium and calcium [32]. Prevalence is reported at about 3-10 percent in the general population, 10-30 percent in type 2 diabetes and higher in hospital and intensive care settings [32]. Because most body magnesium is in bone and tissue, a normal blood level does not rule deficiency out [32]. Mild cases are managed with oral supplements and severe ones with intravenous replacement [32].

Soluble salts such as chloride, citrate and sulfate are absorbed at roughly 30-40 percent, while oxide and hydroxide forms are absorbed less efficiently and more erratically; amino-acid chelates such as glycinate are described as better tolerated, and sustained-release preparations as less likely to cause diarrhoea [30]. A systematic review of supplement bioavailability reached a broadly similar conclusion that organic forms appear more bioavailable than inorganic ones [5]. Specific products are discussed in the wiki's entries on magnesium glycinate and other forms.

Epsom salt takes its name from a well dug on Epsom common in Surrey, England, in 1618; its water was used externally for skin complaints, and Nehemiah Grew's 1695 study of its composition established the salt as a remedy [31]. Today it is sold mainly as bath salts. Wikipedia notes that research on topical magnesium, such as Epsom baths, is very limited and does not describe how much magnesium crosses the skin [31]. Users on looksmax.org ask about magnesium oil for hair [28].

Magnesium ions are cofactors for ATP-dependent enzymes and bind phosphate groups in ATP, DNA and RNA [1]. In the nervous system, magnesium blocks the NMDA subtype of glutamate-gated channel in a voltage-dependent way, a finding that underpins interest in its effects on neural excitability, mood and sleep [16][17]. For bone, magnesium influences calcium handling, parathyroid hormone secretion and vitamin D activation, and is held on the bone mineral surface as a reservoir.

Magnesium is a shiny silvery-white metal of low density that forms a protective oxide layer in air; important compounds include the carbonate, chloride, citrate, hydroxide, oxide and sulfate (Epsom salts) [1][2]. Magnesium and its alloys have also been studied as orthopaedic biomaterials [18].

Magnesium was first recognised as an element by Joseph Black in 1755, and Humphry Davy isolated the pure metal by electrolysis in 1808; the name derives from the mineral magnesia from the Magnesia region of ancient Greece [2]. Epsom salt, a magnesium sulfate, was in medical use from the seventeenth century [31]. Richard Willstätter received the 1915 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for his work on chlorophyll, in which magnesium is the central ion, and later research established magnesium's roles in enzymes, nucleic acids and ion transport; the first three-dimensional structure of a magnesium transport complex was solved in 2004 [30].

Magnesium is among the most commonly taken supplements, sold in many forms including citrate, glycinate and L-threonate, and is popular on social media for sleep and anxiety [8][5]. In physique and bodybuilding forums it is commonly mentioned as an electrolyte important for muscle and nerve function and as part of evening supplement routines, usually alongside zinc, vitamin D or creatine. Industrial uses include lightweight alloys, desulfurisation in steelmaking and pyrotechnics [2].

Wikipedia notes a theorised role for magnesium in testosterone production from cholesterol and a synergy with vitamin D, which are part of why it appears in male-oriented supplement stacks; it also reports that supplementation lowers fasting glucose in people with or at risk of diabetes, and that other associations, such as with depression, are still being studied [30][32].

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, magnesium is discussed as a general-purpose supplement for sleep, energy and recovery, with users sharing forms, combinations and personal outcomes [27][28][29].

claims.claim: Magnesium glycinate with L-theanine and GABA improves sleep, to the point of sleeping very late
claims.believers: A looksmax.org user reports going to sleep at 1 am and waking at 4 pm after taking magnesium glycinate, L-theanine and GABA, and missing an appointment, in a thread titled as saying the combination will make you wake up late [27].
claims.experts: Systematic reviews of randomised trials of magnesium for sleep report heterogeneous findings, and one meta-analysis in older adults found shorter sleep-onset latency [3][6].

claims.claim: Magnesium oil promotes hair growth or reduces hair loss
claims.believers: A looksmax.org thread asks about magnesium oil for hair growth and hair loss [28].
claims.experts: The sources cited on this page do not report trials of topical or oral magnesium for hair outcomes; the evidence they summarise concerns deficiency, sleep, muscle fitness and mood [1][3][4][8].

claims.claim: Magnesium can cure benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV)
claims.believers: A looksmax.org thread is titled "the magnesium that cured my mothers bppv vertigo", presenting a family anecdote [29].
claims.experts: The sources cited on this page do not report trials of magnesium for vertigo; the evidence is described as strongest for correcting a deficiency and limited or mixed for other uses [1][2].

claims.claim: Magnesium before bed improves sleep and next-day recovery
claims.believers: Supplement-stack discussions treat evening magnesium as a relaxant that supports sleep and muscle recovery [27].
claims.experts: Systematic reviews report mixed results for sleep, and a meta-analysis of 14 trials examined effects on muscle fitness [3][4][6].

claims.believers: Forum and supplement-community posts commonly say that many people do not get enough magnesium.
claims.experts: Dietary surveys report about 57 percent of US adults below the recommended intake, while clinical deficiency is reported at roughly 3-10 percent of the general population and a normal blood level does not exclude it [32].

claims.claim: Soaking in Epsom salt or applying magnesium oil delivers magnesium through the skin
claims.believers: Bath-salt and magnesium-oil users say topical magnesium soothes sore muscles.
claims.experts: Wikipedia states that research on topical magnesium is very limited and does not quantify skin absorption [31].
